newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss banks to break secrecy with Holocaust list.
newsitem.headline: Swiss banks to break secrecy with Holocaust list.

text.p: Swiss banks on Wednesday will unveil a long-awaited list of dormant accounts from before 1945, their latest break with banking secrecy under international pressure to find assets left by Holocaust victims.
The Swiss Bankers Association was tightlipped ahead of a news conference set for Wednesday in the capital Berne, when the list and the avenues for its worldwide publication will be made public.
"This is a huge task. We are still working on many of the details," association spokeswoman Silvia Matile said.
The names and account information would appear on the Internet as well as in newspaper ads worldwide, bankers have said.

The list will cover accounts opened by foreigners before World War Two ended in 1945 and whose owners have not been heard from in at least 10 years. These criteria mean the tally could include accounts whose owners dropped out of contact for other reasons than the Holocaust.

A second list will follow in October with dormant pre-1945 accounts opened by Swiss residents, who may have acted as proxies to hide away the assets of European Jews and others threatened by the Nazis.
The news conference was also expected to present details of an independent, international arbitration panel being set up to resolve claims to Holocaust wealth.
By publishing the account details of customers, Swiss banks are making an unprecedented break with a tradition of strict banking privacy.
"This is unprecedented in the world. It is a unique act linked to one of history's most tragic chapters and is aimed at ensuring justice for victims of the Holocaust," Matile said.
Under steady pressure since 1995 from the World Jewish Congress (WJC) and its allies, Swiss banks have gradually retreated from secrecy around World War Two-era business.

Agreements made last year allow two separate commissions of independent researchers into the banks' archives, one seeking assets left by Holocaust victims and another writing a history of neutral Switzerland's role as a wartime financial centre.

But as the matching of lost accounts to present-day heirs remained slow, the banks also agreed to a proposal for the public list from the commission seeking lost assets, a body set up by Swiss banks and the WJC and headed by former U.S. central bank chief Paul Volcker.
The World Jewish Congress said it had mixed feelings about the list.

"We're happy this is finally happening, but we're asking why it has taken so long. From one perspective it has taken 52 years, from our recent perspective it's taken two years," WJC executive director Elan Steinberg told Reuters from New York.
"Certainly there is no suggestion or belief on our part that this is a comprehensive list of dormant accounts," he said.

Steinberg said the list would be based on 1,000 pre-1945 accounts totalling about 43 million Swiss francs ($29.2 million) that the banks found last year. The WJC refuses to recognise this sweep because the banks acted alone, without Jewish or independent experts.
"Unfortunately, given the dimensions of the tragedy of the Holocaust, I expect most of these accounts will be heirless," Steinberg said.
"I also expect that we will very rapidly be able to find heirs following the publication of this list," he added.

Steinberg said nobody knows how much money might be in lost Holocaust accounts, although a figure of up to $7.0 billion has been floated by some critics based on estimates of Nazi assets outside Germany.

"Is it somewhere between 70 million and seven billion dollars? I don't know. But it certainly is far greater than the lowball figure given to us by the Swiss Bankers Association." ($ = 1.472 Swiss Francs)
